title: The boss and the worker
hookLine: authority is service, and work is owed honestly
tomorrow: what do you say to someone who just lost their job?

lines: TEN MORE MINUTES, OFF THE CLOCK.
cards: The schedule drops late again. The manager wants just ten more minutes after you've clocked out. Or flip it around: the coworker who disappears on breaks while the line grows and someone else covers.
Every job is a deal with two sides, and either side can cheat. Jesus speaks to the side with the power first.

teach.h: THE FIRST, THE SERVANT OF ALL.
teach.b: His disciples are arguing about who will be greatest.
He tells them that among the nations, rulers lord it over people, but it isn't to be that way with them: "whosoever will be first among you, shall be the servant of all."
Authority, in that picture, is a job of serving the people under you. And the other side?
When Jesus sends out disciples, he tells them to take what they're given, "for the labourer is worthy of his hire." Pay is owed, not a favor.
Catholic social teaching holds both ends.

Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote that a worker should carry out fully and faithfully the work freely agreed to, and that an employer must never treat workers as mere tools and must give each a just wage.

The Catechism names wrongs on both sides in plain words: paying unjust wages breaks the commandment against stealing, and so does work poorly done. Not a war between bosses and workers, and not blind obedience either.
Each owes the other something real. Here's the thing to tell a friend: in the Catechism, work poorly done and unjust wages sit in the same paragraph.

how: Catholic social teaching, from Pope Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum onward, speaks of just wages and honest work; some Catholics bring their work life to confession, examining both how they lead and how they work.

games.q: what does “the boss and the worker” mean?
o: a contract only lawyers can interpret
a chain of command the worker must obey
two sides of a job, each owing the other

games.q: both sides of the deal — tap the pairs.

s: Catholic teaching simply sides with bosses over workers
it names duties on both sides: a just wage, and honest work.
the Catechism counts work poorly done as a wrong
in the same paragraph as paying unjust wages.
Jesus says whoever would be first must be the servant of all
said to disciples arguing over who was greatest.

games.q: you lead the weekend crew. one worker is great but always ten minutes late. by Mark and the Catechism, what's your move?
o: talk with her honestly and ask what's behind it, as someone who serves the crew.
dock her pay quietly; a boss doesn't owe explanations.
let it go; a good boss never corrects anyone.
games.why: authority is service, and work is owed honestly. a serving boss still names the problem, and asks first.

practice: Think of one person above you and one person beside or below you, at work, school or home. Choose one honest thing you owe each of them: a full effort, a fair word, a thank-you. If it fits, send one of them a short message now.

wordCard.voice: The boss and the worker. Two sides of every job, each owing the other something real.

orig.note: Greek, Mark 10:43: a servant or minister, the role Jesus gives to whoever would be great.

carryVoice: Your line: honest on both sides, service from the top and full effort from the floor. See you tomorrow.
